content.text: The rails hummed before the train was even visible, the way a room quiets before someone important enters it. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close.

A child pressed her whole hand to the glass at a crossing, and a man on a cart waved back at her. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished.

Correspondence written by lamplight in a moving carriage has a particular slant to it, hurried and honest. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down.

We crossed the trestle at walking pace, the river a long way down and entirely indifferent to us. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering.

I will post this at the next stop, if the next stop has anywhere to post a letter at all. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time.

The night train left the platform the way a held breath finally leaves the chest. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun.

I wrote to you from a station whose name I have already forgotten, which tells you something about the station. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight.

The rain on the window turned the passing lamps into long gold smears, and I watched them instead of sleeping. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing.

A conductor two carriages down was singing under his breath, badly, and I found I did not mind. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's. The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried.

We stopped for an hour at a junction with no town attached to it, only a shed and a dog that watched us leave. An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect. The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else.

I have decided that letters written on trains are more honest than letters written at a desk. A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing. The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first.

The line ran along the river for forty miles, close enough that I could hear it under the wheels. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one. The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two.

A woman across the compartment read the same page of her book for three stations running. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least.

The porter at Esting knew my father by name, though my father has been gone from that line for years. An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar. The market square filled slowly and emptied all at once, as though on a signal no one gave aloud.

Somewhere past midnight the carriages grew cold and the other passengers folded themselves smaller against it. A garden gate left open is, more often than not, simply an invitation no one has withdrawn. The lamp oil was rationed that winter, and the evenings grew, by necessity, quieter for it.

I keep meaning to describe the mountains properly and instead I only ever manage the weather in front of them. An old ledger, found later, tells a fuller story than the person who kept it ever meant to leave behind. The wind changed direction twice in a single afternoon, which the fishermen took as its own kind of warning.

At mile two hundred fourteen the telegraph poles are so regular I found myself counting them like a pulse. A long winter makes the first warm day feel larger than the weather alone accounts for. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed.

A soldier travelling home slept the whole way with his cap over his eyes, and no one woke him for his stop. An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be. The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it.

The dining car ran out of tea before Halsworth and the steward apologised as though it were a personal failing. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats.

I have never liked arrivals as much as I like the last hour before one, when everything is still possible. An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting.

A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook. The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished. An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful.

The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall. A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change.

An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can.

The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true. The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before.

A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud. An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been.

The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it.
